articles.title: Artist Sues AI Meme Generator for Selling Deeply Personal Comic as Ad Template
articles.summary: Filipino artist Elmer Saflor sued Memes Apps, alleging its AI meme generator sells subscriptions that reproduce his viral "Running Away Balloon" comic as an ad template without permission. Legal expert Eric Goldman notes precedent favors Saflor, since prior rulings suggest meme use in ads isn't fair use, though proving harm and targeting the generator rather than advertisers could complicate the case. Saflor seeks a court order halting the template's use and an accounting of ad profits, framing the suit as a broader push to protect creators' rights as AI platforms scale.

articles.title: George Clooney, Tom Hanks, and Meryl Streep Back New ‘Human Consent Standard' for AI Licensing
articles.summary: A group of Hollywood actors and producers, including George Clooney, Tom Hanks, and Meryl Streep, are backing a new "Human Consent Standard" letting people set terms for how AI systems use their likeness and creative work. Overseen by the nonprofit RSL Media, the standard builds on last year's Really Simple Licensing Standard and lets AI systems check permissions via robots.txt and a registry launching in June. Unlike RSL, which applies to content at specific URLs, the new standard covers a person's identity, character, or work wherever it appears online.

articles.title: Meta AI is moving into your Threads DMs, where awkward AI chats belong
articles.summary: Meta is moving Meta AI into Threads DMs after feedback showed that many users were uncomfortable interacting with AI publicly in their feeds. Users can privately ask questions about posts, conversations, and other topics, with options to delete chats or mute the AI account. Meta is still testing public Meta AI interactions in the Threads feed in a limited number of countries while it gathers more feedback.

articles.title: How Figma Stays Ahead of Vulnerabilities with Agents
articles.summary: Figma's security team built agentic systems that guard code generation, review pull requests, and audit its decade-old monorepo, all governed by one shared policy. Prioritizing precision over recall proved essential, since historical bugs only measure recall while trust requires developers see mostly valid findings—the team hit 70% precision before enabling PR comments, later reaching 80%. The resulting policy became a de facto threat model, powering hooks that steer secure code generation, adjudication passes that boost recall, and feedback loops that continuously refine detection from bug bounty reports and false-positive dismissals.

articles.title: A Concrete Definition of “Product Sense” (and How to Build It)
articles.summary: As AI takes over more execution work, product sense—the ability to decide what to build—is becoming increasingly valuable, but it requires more than consuming product critiques, research, and industry knowledge. Strong product sense develops by repeatedly completing the full product cycle: understanding problems, making decisions, implementing solutions, measuring outcomes, and reflecting on whether experience-based patterns actually applied. Building reliable intuition therefore requires staying close enough to your work to see its consequences, while recognizing when unfamiliar or misleading situations demand evidence rather than instinct.

articles.title: I Handed a UX Review Over to AI. Here's What Happened
articles.summary: A UX practitioner tested Claude Fable 5 and ChatGPT-5.6 Sol against manual analysis on a real portal review, feeding both models the same brief, research, and analytics data. Both AI models generated reviews filled with irrelevant or invented issues, though Claude proved somewhat more accurate and produced a single coherent document. The author concluded AI works best as a partner grounded in expert-defined heuristics rather than a replacement, and plans to build a custom "agent skill" encoding personal UX judgment for future projects.

articles.title: Turn Any Video or Audio Into Accurate Text (Website)
articles.summary: Voqusa is a free AI transcript tool that converts videos from TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, Twitter/X, LinkedIn, and Pinterest into text.

articles.title: AI Nudges, Biases & Heuristics (Website)
articles.summary: 45 interactive field cards covering nudges, biases, heuristics, and AI phenomena. A practical reference for designers, researchers, and product teams building with AI.

articles.title: Accessibility is Resistance!
articles.summary: A blind author explains why they rely heavily on AI tools, using an inaccessible EAA document and image-poor product pages as examples. Screen readers, ChatGPT/Claude, Meta Ray-Bans, and apps like Oorion help them navigate text, describe images, and locate objects independently. They distinguish "AI as augmentation" from "AI as compensation," arguing better human-built accessibility would reduce reliance on AI, and urge readers to prioritize accessibility as a form of resistance.

articles.title: Playful Retail is Serious Design Work
articles.summary: Interactive retail spaces that feel spontaneous, like the Coach Charm Playground at Selfridges, actually require immense hidden planning and discipline to execute safely and smoothly, according to Studio XAG. The project involved navigating regulations, testing over 150 sample sets, and executing overnight installs with precision compared to a Formula One pit stop. Key lessons highlighted include protecting the core idea through production, learning from workshop fabricators, and prioritizing real human behavior over portfolio aesthetics.

articles.title: Disney's Ozzy Fox is Going Viral Thanks to 'AI Slop' Accusations
articles.summary: Disney's new preschool cartoon "Ozzy Fox" went viral after viewers accused it of being "AI slop," despite the show not actually using generative AI.

articles.title: Stats Show LinkedIn's ‘Open to Work' Badge Works. Designers Say it Could be Even Better
articles.summary: LinkedIn's "Open to Work" badge, active for six years, resurfaced as a debate topic after an engineer's viral X post called it a negative signal to recruiters.
